subject: Examplapay performance alignment — first-chunk window & streaming
messages:
From: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwoodinference.com>
To: Sana Ahmed <sana@examplapay.com>
Cc: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwoodinference.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-06-10T18:12:00Z
Subject: Post-call recap — Examplapay performance alignment

Hi Sana / Michael,

Thanks again for the call today — appreciate the clear runway you gave us. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned on the performance targets and assumptions we discussed. Please flag anything I missed.

Key performance targets you stated on the call:
- Initial response target: 150 ms P95 for the web app’s first chunk (your \"first-chunk window\") — important for perceived latency on the search UI.
- Streaming mode: prefer SSE for desktop/web; mobile app may use WebSocket for multiplexing.
- Chunk cadence: target 80–200 ms between chunks for progressive rendering (smaller chunks for tokenized responses).
- Concurrency: baseline 600 concurrent active sessions (~peak 200 RPS sustained, bursts to 1k).
- Throughput: average payload ~120 tokens generated per request; peak growth scenarios up to 3x over first 6 months.

Open items / assumptions for validation:
1) Burst behavior: do bursts map to short-lived spikes (seconds) or sustained (minutes)? (affects autoscale config).
2) Typical prompt size and stop sequences — we need average and 95th percentile token counts for both prompt and expected response.
3) Authentication pattern — are you terminating at edge (Cloud CDN) or passing direct to our private endpoint?
4) Failure policy — do you prefer graceful degrade to a cheaper smaller model or queueing with client-side backoff?

What Redwood recommends as the immediate next steps:
- Action A: You provide a short CSV with sample request shapes (timestamp, prompt_token_count, expected_response_token_count, client_type). This lets us size batch windows and KV cache expectations.
- Action B: We’ll provision a short-lived Dedicated pilot environment (2 GPUs) and run a 48–72 hour profile using replayed traffic to validate TTFT and chunk cadence under your concurrency mix.
- Action C: Soojin will propose a concrete autopilot config (batch size limits, prefix cache TTLs, pre-warm policies) and a fall-back policy for model downgrades to keep UX reasonable during high contention.

Attachments: none from us for now — we can share a sample perf template if useful.

Proposed timeline:
- You send sample traffic and confirm burst characteristics by Thu 2026-06-11.
- We spin pilot and return a preliminary runbook and dashboard within 72 hours of receiving samples.

Thanks — I’ll follow up with specific pilot details once we have the CSV.

Cheers,
Dylan Brooks
Enterprise Account Executive
Redwood Inference

Date: 2026-06-11T08:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — Examplapay performance alignment

Thanks Dylan — good summary. A few clarifications from our side:

- The 150 ms target was aspirational; after internal sync we think 180–200 ms P95 for first chunk is acceptable to product, as long as consistency is good across regions.
- Bursts are typically short (10–90s) but frequent during peak minutes; occasional large spikes during promotional events (could be several minutes).
- Average prompt tokens: 40 (p50), response tokens: 110 (p50); p95 response tokens ~360.
- Auth: traffic goes through our edge proxy (Akamai) and we terminate TLS there; we can route certain paths to your private endpoint but want to minimize double TLS hops.
- Fallbacks: prefer graceful degrade to smaller model (same family) with explicit client flag so we can instrument UX change.

I’ve attached our perf sheet with sample traffic rows and the product team’s acceptable ranges (examplapay-perf-requirements.xlsx). Also tagging Michael (CTO) — he’s interested in whether SSE and WebSocket have different operational implications for long-lived connections in our mobile fleet.

One question: do you have a recommended packet/chunk size (in bytes or tokens) we should aim for to balance TTFT vs. server CPU?

Thanks,
Sana Ahmed
Product Ops Manager
Examplapay

--
Attachment: examplapay-perf-requirements.xlsx (spreadsheet, 48KB)
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwoodinference.com>

Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-06-11T16:42:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — Examplapay performance alignment

Hi Sana — thanks for the sheet and the clarifications. Quick technical notes and a suggested pilot plan.

Technical answers / recommendations:
- Chunk size: aim for ~16–64 tokens per chunk for natural-language streaming; this typically maps to 200–800 bytes depending on encoding. Smaller chunks (16–32 tokens) improve perceived TTFT but increase per-chunk overhead.
- For TTFT: prefix/KV caching provides the biggest win for repeated prompts (we can often shave 40–70% off initial compute for cached prefixes). If you have repeated system prompts, we’ll advise pinning those in the cache.
- SSE vs WebSocket: SSE is simpler for browser flows and plays nicely with CDN edge caching for static responses; WebSocket reduces handshake cost for long-lived mobile multiplexed connections. Operational differences: WebSockets require sticky routing and are more likely to keep an open socket to a single host; SSE works well with our streaming fronting and is easier to scale behind load balancers.
- Autoscale and burst handling: we recommend a hybrid model — a small baseline Dedicated pool sized for 200 RPS steady state + burst autoscale to a larger pool (policy-based) with faster pre-warm when predicted by traffic signals.

Pilot proposal (what we’ll run if you approve):
1) Provision a 72-hour Dedicated pilot attached to a sandbox key.
2) Replay your CSV traffic at a 1:1 scale for 24h, then a 2x stress window (1 hour) to observe burst behavior.
3) Collect P95 TTFT, per-chunk inter-arrival times, CPU/gpu utilization, and prefix cache hit rates.
4) Optional: run an SSE vs WS smoke to measure differences in connection stability under your mobile NAT topologies.

Artifacts we’ll need from you before pilot start:
- The CSV you attached (good) plus a separate sample of the largest expected request payloads (top-10 heavy requests).
- A test service account and an IP allowlist for our pilot runners.

I’m attaching a short decision matrix we often share when teams choose SSE vs WS: sse-vs-ws-decision-matrix.pdf (lightweight).

If that plan looks good, I’ll open the pilot ticket and propose concrete instance types and a tentative pilot start time.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
